mainEntity.name: How much does a BMW 7 Series 725tds engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A BMW 7 Series 725tds engine replacement typically costs £900-£1,800 for a used M51D25 unit, £1,800-£3,200 for a reconditioned engine, and £2,500-£4,000 for a fully rebuilt engine with warranty. Supply & fit adds £520-£715 in specialist labour (8-11 hours). Used engines offer the lowest upfront cost with limited warranty; reconditioned engines sit in the mid-range with some new parts fitted; rebuilt engines are the most expensive but fully restored to factory spec with a 12-month warranty.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of injection pump failure in a BMW 7 Series 725tds?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common symptoms include difficulty starting when cold, rough idling, loss of power under load, and black or grey smoke from the exhaust. In advanced cases, the engine may crank but fail to start entirely. If you suspect injection pump issues, have it tested by a Bosch diesel specialist immediately - failing pumps can contaminate injectors and fuel lines.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a BMW 7 Series 725tds?

acceptedAnswer.text: With average values of £2,500-£4,500, a full rebuilt engine at £2,500-£4,000 represents a significant investment. However, if your 725tds is in excellent condition with low mileage and good bodywork, a rebuilt engine can extend its life by 150,000+ miles - often cheaper than buying a replacement classic of similar condition. For sub-£3,000 cars, consider a used engine or targeted repair; for £3,000-£4,500 cars, a reconditioned engine is viable; for £4,500+ cars, a rebuilt engine with warranty makes strong financial sense.

mainEntity.name: How long does a BMW 7 Series 725tds engine replacement take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A typical BMW 7 Series 725tds engine replacement takes 2-4 days for supply and fit at a specialist garage. The M51D25 is a straight-six with good engine bay access on the E38, but the job still requires removing the front end and gearbox. Most specialists offer collection/delivery options nationwide with same-day dispatch available for in-stock engines.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the BMW 725tds and 730d engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 725tds uses the 2.5L M51D25 six-cylinder diesel (143hp, 280Nm), while the 730d (introduced in 1998) uses the 3.0L M57D30 six-cylinder diesel (184hp, 390Nm). The 730d offers significantly more power and torque, but the 725tds is lighter on fuel and carries lower replacement costs.

The M51D25 is considered one of BMW's more robust diesel engines, with many examples exceeding 200,000-300,000 miles when properly maintained. The key to longevity is regular oil changes, using the correct diesel fuel and maintaining the injection system, and addressing turbo or boost leaks early.

historyTimeline.h2: BMW 7 Series 725tds - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The BMW 725tds joined the E38 7 Series range in March 1996 as the brand's first diesel model in the luxury class. Powered by the M51D25 six-cylinder turbo-diesel, the 725tds brought diesel efficiency and torque to BMW's flagship saloon - paving the way for the 730d and 740d that followed in 1998 and 1999. The 725tds remained in production until February 2000, when the E38 generation ended.

milestones.description: March 1996 - M51D25, 2.5L six-cylinder turbo-diesel, 143hp, introduced as BMW's first diesel 7 Series
E38 facelift (LCI) introduced; 725tds continues with updated styling
February 2000 - E38 7 Series production ends; the 725tds is not carried forward to the E65 generation

Rebuilt M51D25 engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: Injection Pump Failure - Why the BMW 7 Series 725tds M51D25 Suffers Starting and Running Issues
problems.rootCause: The M51D25 uses a Bosch VP37 mechanical injection pump. Over time, internal seals can degrade, allowing fuel to bypass internal components. This leads to poor cold starting, rough idling, loss of power, and in severe cases, complete failure to start. Fuel contamination from degraded seals can also damage injectors.

Boost leaks from perished rubber hoses and intercooler pipework are also common on ageing examples, leading to reduced power, increased fuel consumption, and black smoke from the exhaust.
